nav.look.title: Looking around
nav.look.intro: Two commands tell you where you are and what is here.

examples.desc: shows the folder you are in, like /home/you
lists the files and folders here
also shows hidden files (names starting with .)

nav.look.tip: You can't break anything by looking — explore freely.

nav.move.title: cd — move between folders
nav.move.intro: cd means “change directory” (a directory is a folder).

examples.desc: go into the folder named games
go up one folder, toward home
jump straight back to your home folder

nav.read.title: cat — read a file
nav.read.intro: cat prints everything inside a text file.

examples.desc: shows what is written in welcome.txt
reads a file inside the box folder

nav.read.tip: A name like notes.txt has a name (notes) and a type (.txt = text).

nav.map.title: tree — the whole map
nav.map.intro: tree draws all the folders and files as a branching map.

examples.desc: shows every folder and file from here down

nav.map.tip: Great for seeing where everything lives at a glance.

make.create.title: mkdir & touch — make things
make.create.intro: mkdir makes a new folder; touch makes a new empty file.

examples.desc: makes a folder named toys
makes an empty file ball.txt inside toys

make.create.tip: Build folders inside folders: mkdir city, then mkdir city/park.

make.write.title: echo and > — write into a file
make.write.intro: echo prints text. Add > to send that text INTO a file.

examples.desc: just prints hello on the screen
puts hello INTO note.txt (replaces it)
ADDS a line to the end of note.txt

make.write.tip: > replaces the file, >> adds to the end.

make.copy.title: cp & mv — copy and rename
make.copy.intro: cp copies a file; mv moves or renames it.

examples.desc: makes a copy called b.txt
renames b.txt to c.txt
moves c.txt into the box folder

make.copy.tip: cp keeps the first file, mv does not.

make.remove.title: rm — delete (carefully)
make.remove.intro: rm removes a file. To delete a whole folder, add the -r flag.

examples.desc: deletes the file old.txt
deletes a folder and everything in it

make.remove.tip: A flag is an extra option that starts with a dash, like -r. Here it's safe; on a real computer rm is forever.

seek.find.title: find — search by name
seek.find.intro: find looks for a file anywhere below you, by its name.

examples.desc: finds where ball.txt is hiding
finds names that contain toy (* means anything)

seek.find.tip: find looks at names; grep (next) looks INSIDE files.

seek.grep.title: grep — search inside files
seek.grep.intro: grep searches for a word inside files.

examples.desc: finds the word treasure in any file here
searches only inside diary.txt

seek.grep.tip: grep is how you find which file mentions something.

seek.star.title: The * wildcard
seek.star.intro: * means “anything”, so you can match many files at once.

examples.desc: lists only the text files
finds names with toy anywhere in them

seek.star.tip: Mix * with other commands to work on lots of files at once.

view.peek.title: head & tail — peek at a file
view.peek.intro: head shows the FIRST lines, tail shows the LAST lines.

examples.desc: shows the first few lines
shows the last few lines

view.peek.tip: Handy for long files when you don't want all of it.

view.count.title: wc — count a file
view.count.intro: wc counts the lines, words and letters in a file.

examples.desc: prints: lines words letters  poem.txt

order.sort.title: sort — put lines in order
order.sort.intro: sort shows a file's lines in A-Z (or number) order.

examples.desc: shows the animals in A-Z order

order.sort.tip: sort doesn't change the file, it just shows it sorted.

order.uniq.title: uniq — remove repeats
order.uniq.intro: uniq removes repeated lines that are next to each other.

examples.desc: drops side-by-side duplicate lines

order.uniq.tip: Tip: sort first, then uniq, to remove ALL duplicates.

flip.rev.title: rev — flip text
flip.rev.intro: rev flips each line of text backwards, letter by letter.

examples.desc: prints every line reversed, olleh -> hello

flip.rev.tip: Silly and fun — great for secret messages.

flip.shout.title: tr — swap letters
flip.shout.intro: tr swaps one set of letters for another.

examples.desc: turns small letters into BIG ones (SHOUTING)
changes every o into a 0

flip.shout.tip: tr means “translate” — swap these for those.

slice.cut.title: cut — take part of a line
slice.cut.intro: cut keeps only part of each line.

examples.desc: keeps the first 3 letters of each line
keeps the first word of each line

slice.nl.title: nl — number the lines
slice.nl.intro: nl puts a line number in front of every line.

examples.desc: 1  first line, 2  second line, ...

slice.nl.tip: Great for talking about “line 3” of a file.

pipe.first.title: Pipes | — join commands
pipe.first.intro: A pipe | sends one command's output straight INTO the next one.

examples.desc: read the file, then sort it
read, sort, then remove repeats
read, then count it

pipe.first.tip: Think of | as a water pipe carrying text from one command to the next.

vars.set.title: Variables — boxes for words
vars.set.intro: A variable is a labelled box that holds a word. Write name=value (no spaces).

examples.desc: puts dragon into a box named pet
shows what's in the box: dragon

vars.who.title: whoami, $USER, date
vars.who.intro: The computer already knows a few things about you.

examples.desc: prints your name
your name, from a ready-made variable
shows the date and time

vars.who.tip: $USER is a box that already has your name in it.

guard.look.title: ls -l & id — details
guard.look.intro: ls -l shows file details (who may change them); id shows who YOU are.

examples.desc: lists files with a details column
shows your user and groups

guard.look.tip: The details tell you if a file is locked or open.

guard.lock.title: chmod — lock a file
guard.lock.intro: chmod can lock a file so it can't be changed, or unlock it again.

examples.desc: locks vault.txt (no changes allowed)
unlocks vault.txt again

guard.lock.tip: Try to delete a locked file and the computer will politely refuse.

depth.du.title: du — how big?
depth.du.intro: du measures how big a file or folder is.

examples.desc: shows the size of poem.txt

depth.df.title: df — disk space
depth.df.intro: df shows how much room is left on the whole disk.

examples.desc: shows total, used and free space

depth.stat.title: stat — full info
depth.stat.intro: stat shows everything about a file: type, size and lock.

examples.desc: name, type, size and lock status

depth.stat.tip: stat is like an ID card for a file.

motor.ps.title: ps — running programs
motor.ps.intro: ps lists the little programs running right now, each with a number (PID).

examples.desc: shows PID and name of each program

motor.ps.tip: PID means “process id” — a program's number.

motor.kill.title: kill — stop a program
motor.kill.intro: kill stops a running program by its number (PID).

examples.desc: stops the program whose PID is 77

motor.kill.tip: Use ps first to see the PIDs, then kill the one you want.

panel.env.title: env & $PATH — settings
panel.env.intro: env lists the computer's settings (its variables). $PATH is where commands live.

examples.desc: lists all the settings
shows the list of places commands are kept

panel.env.tip: Settings are just variables the whole computer shares.

panel.which.title: which — where is it?
panel.which.intro: which tells you where a command program lives.

examples.desc: prints the path to grep, like /bin/grep

panel.which.tip: Every command is really a little program stored somewhere.

radio.ping.title: ping — are you awake?
radio.ping.intro: ping asks another computer “are you there?” and waits for a reply.

examples.desc: sends hellos and shows the replies

radio.ping.tip: If it replies, that computer is awake and reachable.

radio.curl.title: curl — fetch a page
radio.curl.intro: curl fetches a page of text from another computer.

examples.desc: downloads and shows that page

radio.curl.tip: A web page is really just a file on another computer.

spell.make.title: Scripts — a spell book
spell.make.intro: A script is a file full of commands. Write the lines with echo and >, >>.

examples.desc: start spell.sh with the line whoami
add a second line, ls

spell.make.tip: A .sh file is a script you can run again and again.

spell.run.title: run — cast the spell
spell.run.intro: run does every line in a script file for you, top to bottom.

examples.desc: runs all the commands inside spell.sh

spell.run.tip: Write it once, run it a hundred times.

spell.repeat.title: repeat — do it many times
spell.repeat.intro: repeat does the same command several times in a row.

examples.desc: prints hi three times

spell.repeat.tip: Computers are great at doing boring things many times.
